claims.text: MTP+FEP will reduce the computational cost of calculating the TaVCrW melting temperature by more than 80%.
MTP+FEP will keep the free-energy difference within 0.5 meV/atom of the TOR-TILD baseline.
Achieving the proposed accuracy requires an MTP trained on a phase-space distribution that captures SRO.
SRO stabilizes the TaVCrW solid by approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
The initial TaVCrW state is a random solid solution that may contain SRO clusters.
The EAM reference and thermodynamic integration are to be replaced by an MTP and free-energy perturbation.
The method is to be evaluated over 2000-2400 K.
A supercell with an SRO length scale greater than 1.2 nm is needed.
An MTP cutoff of about 4.7 Å and maximum level 14 is suitable for reproducing the relevant TaVCrW phase-space distribution.
Accurate reproduction of the ab initio phase-space distribution by the MTP enables FEP to converge without the extensive sampling required by TI.
The MTP retains energetic penalties associated with breaking SRO, analogous to a DAPB energy in MoNbTaW.
The MTP retains the high-temperature entropy terms relevant to the free energy.
FEP can obtain the solid-liquid free-energy difference directly from a limited number of configurations and thereby bypass slow TI convergence.
The MTP+FEP melting temperature for TaVCrW will agree with TOR-TILD within 10 K.
A standard EAM without SRO training will fail to capture the proposed SRO-induced free-energy shift.
Large or percolating SRO clusters produce stronger observable effects than small clusters.
SRO strengthening of screw dislocations in MoNbTaW attenuates with temperature and is negligible around 2000 K.
V and Cr deviate at 0 K from standard GGA-PBE/LDA underbinding or overbinding rules.
A ground-state-trained MTP may omit electronic entropy, electronic-excitation, and high-temperature magnetic-fluctuation effects.
The method is falsified if its free energy differs from TOR-TILD by more than 0.5 meV/atom at any tested temperature or if its cost reduction is below 80% while meeting the accuracy requirement.
